<reason>A kept one coherent decision rule — ex ante consent is the only verifiable control against an irreversible taking — and answered both pressure questions directly and substantively (de-identification plus a categorical orphan-works exception for unreachable parties; purpose-and-beneficiary plus possession-≠-license for the spam-filter challenge). B landed real hits: the incumbent-moat/grandfathering point, the "manufactured yes" critique of consent dialogs, and the smart-reply trap. But B's alternative regime stayed abstract ("documented low-risk conditions"), its post-hoc remedies never answered A's unverifiability charge ("no one can verify what a model has forgotten"), its own framework also leaves already-taken data with giants (exposed by A's Q2), and the overbreadth point was dropped after R1. B also lost material to two clippings, including the closing section of Rebuttal 2. A's closing did the cleaner comparative weighing (the de-identification horns; who chooses, and when), while B's closing mostly reasserted.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 2 smart-reply trap: A's provider-exception defense of spam filtering also covers service-improving training on private mail, so A's line collapses into the purpose/risk judgment that is B's regime — the most damaging single move of the debate. A's closing partially saved it ("platforms have users and can ask; only a firm with no relationship to the people cannot ask — that is the motion"), which is exactly the kind of exchange that decided this: B kept landing traps, A kept having answers, and B's own escape routes were never squared with the irreversibility problem.</best_rebuttal>
